story: Around 500 AD, the brilliant Nazca civilization of southern Peru met a quiet, self-inflicted doom. Famous for carving massive, intricate geoglyphs of animals and straight lines into the desert floor, the Nazca people gradually cleared out the native Huarango trees to make room for expanding maize and cotton agriculture. They could not know that these deep-rooted trees were the ecological keystone holding the fragile desert landscape together. When a catastrophic El Niño cycle struck around 500 AD, unleashing torrential flooding, the unprotected soil simply washed away. The rivers cut deep into the floodplain, leaving the Nazca's sophisticated underground aqueducts high and dry. Their thriving society collapsed into a salty, barren desert, leaving behind giant animal figures visible only from the sky as a silent monument to ecological overreach.
angle: The world-famous Nazca Lines were built by a civilization that accidentally triggered its own collapse by cutting down the one tree holding their desert floor together.

claims.claim: The Nazca lines are massive geoglyphs created by removing the top 12 to 15 inches of dark, oxidized surface rocks to reveal lighter sand underneath.
The combined length of the Nazca lines is more than 1,300 km (800 mi), covering an area of about 50 km2 to over 450 km2.
The civilization started to decline from 500 AD and had fallen completely by 750 AD.
The demise of the Nazca society was linked to the destruction of forests containing the Huarango tree (Prosopis pallida).
The Huarango is an ecological keystone species in the desert zone with one of the deepest root systems, enhancing soil fertility and moisture.
The clearing of woodland was driven by an increasing population and a greater need for food, particularly for maize and cotton agriculture.
An El Niño event around 500 AD triggered severe flooding along the coast of Peru.
Without sufficient Huarango tree cover, the landscape was exposed to catastrophic erosion from the El Niño floods.
The river down-cut into its floodplain, leaving the Nazca irrigation systems and aqueducts high and dry.
The region receives very little rainfall, averaging around 20 minutes or less than an inch of rain per year.

disputed: The exact purpose of the Nazca lines, whether astronomical calendars, water ritual paths, or constellation maps, remains debated among scholars and should be attributed.
Erich von Däniken's pseudoscientific theory that the lines were ancient astronaut landing sites is refuted by scientists and should be dismissed or labeled as fringe speculation.
